items.prompt: What is an allele?

options.label: A section of DNA with no function
A type of chromosome in gametes
One version of the same gene
A protein that copies a gene

rubric: An allele is one of the alternative versions of a gene.
Distractors confuse alleles with junk DNA, enzymes or chromosome types.

items.prompt: A person has the genotype Aa. What is the term for this genotype?

options.label: Homozygous recessive
Homozygous dominant
Hemizygous
Heterozygous

rubric: Two different alleles make a heterozygous genotype.
Homozygous options are chosen by learners who confuse same and different alleles.

items.prompt: How many chromosomes are in a typical human body (somatic) cell?
rubric: Human somatic cells have 46 chromosomes, in 23 pairs.
23 is the gamete number; 92 is the count after DNA replication.

items.prompt: What does Mendel's law of segregation state?

options.label: Dominant alleles become more common in a population over time
The two alleles of a gene separate into different gametes
Each gamete receives both alleles of every gene in the parent
Genes on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together

rubric: Segregation means the two alleles separate during gamete formation.
Distractors mix up linkage, population change and the diploid condition.

items.prompt: What is a phenotype?

options.label: The ratio of offspring in a cross
The pair of alleles an organism carries
The order of bases in a gene
The observable trait of an organism

rubric: Phenotype is the observable characteristic.
Genotype (the allele pair) is the most common confusion.

items.prompt: Which of the following are nitrogenous bases found in DNA? Select all that apply.

options.label: Ribose
Thymine
Uracil
Adenine
Cytosine

rubric: DNA bases are adenine, thymine, cytosine and guanine.
Uracil is found in RNA, and ribose is a sugar, not a base.

items.prompt: A clinic report lists a newborn's karyotype as 46,XY. A nurse is asked to name the baby's sex chromosomes.

options.label: Two X chromosomes, one from each parent
Two Y chromosomes, one from each parent
One X chromosome only, with no second sex chromosome
One X and one Y chromosome

rubric: XY means one X and one Y, the typical male pattern.
XX is the typical female pattern; X only describes a different condition.

items.prompt: In pea plants, tall (T) is dominant to short (t). Why does a Tt plant look tall?

options.label: The plant gets taller because it has two different alleles
The T allele masks the effect of the t allele
The t allele is lost during development
The two alleles blend to give a medium height

rubric: A dominant allele determines the phenotype in heterozygotes.
Blending is the incorrect idea of incomplete dominance.

items.prompt: Why can a recessive trait appear to skip a generation?

options.label: The trait is switched off in every second generation of a family line
The recessive allele is lost in the middle generation and later mutates back
Recessive alleles are only passed on by grandparents to their grandchildren
Carriers with one recessive allele show no trait but pass it on

rubric: Heterozygous carriers hide the allele and can transmit it.
Distractors invent disappearance or generation-based rules.

items.prompt: Why are X-linked recessive conditions more often seen in males than in females?

options.label: Females cannot inherit X-linked genes from fathers
Males have two X chromosomes, which doubles the risk
The Y chromosome carries the same allele as the X
Males have one X, so one recessive allele shows

rubric: Males have only one X, so a single recessive allele is expressed.
Distractors reverse the chromosome counts or deny inheritance.

items.prompt: A mutation occurs in a skin cell of an adult. Why is it very unlikely to be passed to the person's children?

options.label: Skin cells are not gametes, so it is not in sperm or eggs
Skin cell mutations are usually repaired before the person has children
Children inherit mostly dominant mutations from their parents' body cells
Mutations in skin cells change proteins but not the DNA sequence itself

rubric: Only mutations in germ-line cells are inherited.
Learners wrongly think all mutations are inherited or repaired.

items.prompt: A person has blood type AB, with both A and B markers on red cells. Which pattern of inheritance does this show?

options.label: Sex linkage, where the gene is on the X
Codominance, where both alleles are expressed
Complete dominance, where one allele masks the other
Incomplete dominance, where a blend appears

rubric: Both alleles are fully expressed in codominance.
Incomplete dominance gives an intermediate blend, not two distinct markers.

items.prompt: Which statements correctly explain how meiosis increases genetic variation? Select all that apply.

options.label: DNA is copied twice before the cells divide
Crossing over swaps segments between homologous chromosomes
Meiosis produces cells identical to the parent cell
Independent assortment shuffles which chromosomes go to each gamete

rubric: Crossing over and independent assortment create new allele combinations.
Identical cells describe mitosis; DNA is copied once, not twice.

items.prompt: A family pedigree shows two unaffected parents who have a child with a genetic condition. A student must decide what this suggests about how the condition is inherited.

options.label: It is dominant, and both parents carry a hidden copy that skipped them
It is caused by a new mutation in the child's body cells after birth
It is Y-linked, because the child is affected and fathers pass on the Y
It is recessive, and both parents are likely carriers

rubric: Unaffected parents with an affected child indicates a recessive trait with carrier parents.
A dominant trait would show in at least one parent.

items.prompt: What does it mean to say an allele is recessive?

options.label: It is usually less common than the dominant allele in a population
It is a mutated copy of a gene that lowers fitness
It is carried on the X chromosome rather than an autosome
Its effect is hidden in heterozygotes by the dominant allele

rubric: A recessive allele only shows in the phenotype when no dominant allele is present.
Distractors confuse dominance with frequency, sex linkage or harmfulness.

items.prompt: According to Mendel's law of segregation, what happens to the two alleles of a gene when gametes form?

options.label: They stay paired so each gamete carries both alleles
They separate so each gamete carries only one allele
They blend together into one intermediate allele
They are copied so each gamete carries four alleles

rubric: Alleles separate during meiosis so each gamete gets one copy.
Distractors reflect blending inheritance or misunderstanding of gamete content.

items.prompt: Two unaffected parents have an affected daughter. Which inheritance mode does this best indicate?

options.label: X-linked dominant
Autosomal dominant
Y-linked
Autosomal recessive

rubric: Unaffected carriers can both pass a recessive allele to a child of either sex.
Dominant and Y-linked traits would require an affected parent; a daughter cannot inherit a Y-linked trait.

items.prompt: Why do two genes that are linked often fail to assort independently?

options.label: They sit close together on the same chromosome, so they tend to be inherited as a unit
They are both on sex chromosomes, so they are always passed on to sons together
They are on homologous chromosomes of different sizes, so they pair incorrectly in meiosis
They both carry dominant alleles, so one gene copies the other into gametes

rubric: Genes close together on one chromosome rarely get separated by crossing over.
Distractors invent pairing errors, copying or sex-chromosome explanations.

items.prompt: A single base change alters a codon, but the amino acid in the protein stays the same. How is this mutation classified?

options.label: Frameshift
Missense
Nonsense
Silent

rubric: Redundancy of the genetic code means some changes do not alter the amino acid, which is a silent mutation.
Missense changes the amino acid, nonsense creates a stop, frameshift shifts the reading frame.

items.prompt: Which statements are consistent with X-linked recessive inheritance? Select all that apply.

options.label: An affected father cannot pass the trait directly to his sons
Affected males are more common than affected females
A carrier mother can have an affected son
An affected father always has affected sons

rubric: Males have one X, so one recessive allele shows; sons get their X from their mother, not their father.
The last option wrongly assumes fathers pass the X-linked allele to sons.

items.prompt: A family history shows a trait in every generation. About half the children of an affected parent are affected, both sons and daughters, and one affected father has an affected son. Which inheritance pattern fits best?

options.label: Autosomal recessive
X-linked recessive
Mitochondrial inheritance
Autosomal dominant

rubric: Appearing every generation with male-to-male transmission and both sexes affected suggests autosomal dominant.
Mitochondrial traits come from mothers only; X-linked traits cannot pass father to son; recessive traits skip generations.

items.prompt: Two heterozygous parents (Aa x Aa) have a child. What is the probability the child is aa?
rubric: Punnett square gives 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa.
1/2 is the heterozygote fraction; 3/4 is the dominant phenotype fraction.

items.prompt: A heterozygous tall pea plant (Tt) is test-crossed with a short plant (tt). What fraction of offspring is expected to be tall?

options.label: All

rubric: Tt x tt gives half Tt (tall) and half tt (short).
1/4 and 3/4 come from misapplying the Tt x Tt ratios.

items.prompt: Two plants are both AaBb, with the genes assorting independently. What is the probability an offspring is aabb?
rubric: Multiply 1/4 for aa by 1/4 for bb to get 1/16.
Other options come from adding probabilities or using the 9:3:3:1 numerators wrongly.

items.prompt: In a population at Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, 1 in 25 people has a recessive disorder (q^2 = 0.04). What fraction of people are carriers (2pq)?
rubric: 0.16 and 0.04 come from using q or q^2 for carriers; 0.64 is p^2.

items.prompt: Red snapdragons (RR) crossed with white (WW) give pink F1 (RW) by incomplete dominance. Two pink F1 plants are crossed. What is the phenotype ratio of their offspring?

options.label: 1 pink : 1 white
All pink offspring
3 red : 1 white, as dominance
1 red : 2 pink : 1 white

rubric: RW x RW gives 1 RR : 2 RW : 1 rr-type genotypes, each with its own phenotype.
3:1 wrongly assumes complete dominance.

items.prompt: ABO blood type is controlled by alleles IA, IB and i (i is recessive). Which parental genotype pairs can produce a child with type O blood? Select all that apply.

options.label: IAIA x ii
IAi x IAi
IAi x IBi
IBIB x IAi

rubric: Type O needs ii, so both parents must carry an i allele.
IAIA and IBIB parents cannot pass i.

items.prompt: Red-green colour blindness is X-linked recessive. A woman with normal vision whose father was colour blind (a carrier, XCXc) has children with a man with normal vision (XCY). What is the probability that any given child is a colour-blind son?
rubric: Half the children are sons, and half of those get Xc from the mother, so 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4.
1/2 is the chance a son is affected, not a child being an affected son.

items.prompt: In pea plants, tall (T) is dominant to short (t) and purple flowers (P) are dominant to white (p); the genes assort independently. A cross of TtPp x ttpp is made. What fraction of offspring is expected to be tall with white flowers?
rubric: Testcross gives 1/2 tall x 1/2 white = 1/4.
3/16 comes from wrongly applying a dihybrid-cross ratio to a testcross.

items.prompt: A woman is a carrier of an X-linked recessive allele for red-green colour blindness. Her husband has normal colour vision. What is the probability that a son of theirs is colour blind?
rubric: Sons receive the mother's X; half carry the allele, so 1/2.
1/4 confuses the chance with that for any child, ignoring that the question is about sons only.

items.prompt: In a population in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, 16% of individuals show a recessive trait (genotype aa). What is the expected frequency of heterozygous carriers (Aa)?
rubric: 24% uses pq and omits the factor of 2.

items.prompt: Two genes are 20 map units apart on one chromosome. An individual with genotype AB/ab (alleles in cis) is testcrossed to ab/ab. What proportion of the offspring is expected to be recombinant?
rubric: Map units equal percent recombinants, so 20%.
10% is the frequency of each single recombinant class, not the total.

items.prompt: Both parents are heterozygous carriers (Aa) of an autosomal recessive disorder. They plan to have two children. What is the probability that both children are affected?
rubric: Each child has 1/4 chance, so 1/4 x 1/4 = 1/16.
1/4 ignores that the two independent events must be multiplied.

items.prompt: A man with blood type AB and a woman with blood type O have a child. Which blood types could the child have? Select all that apply.

options.label: Type AB
Type B
Type A
Type O

rubric: The woman gives only i; the man gives IA or IB, so A or B.
AB and O are tempting if you forget that the O parent contributes only i.

items.prompt: A genetic counsellor is told that a couple's first child has cystic fibrosis (autosomal recessive). Both parents are unaffected. The couple now asks about their second pregnancy. What is the probability that the second child is affected?
rubric: Both parents must be carriers; each pregnancy is independent with 1/4 risk.
1/16 wrongly multiplies the risk again, treating the first child as part of the second child's chance.

items.prompt: A testcross of a dihybrid yields 42% AB, 42% ab, 8% Ab and 8% aB. What is the best interpretation?

options.label: The genes assort independently because all four classes appear
The genes are linked, 16 map units apart, with alleles in cis
The genes are linked, about 84 map units apart, with alleles in cis, since parental types are the most common classes
The genes are linked, about 8 map units apart, with alleles in trans

rubric: Recombinants total 16%, parental types are most common, so cis arrangement.
Taking 8% as the distance counts only one recombinant class.

items.prompt: A pedigree shows an affected father who has affected daughters, but none of his sons are affected. Affected mothers pass the trait to about half their children of both sexes. Which inheritance pattern fits best?

options.label: X-linked dominant
Y-linked
X-linked recessive
Autosomal recessive

rubric: Fathers pass their X to all daughters and none to sons, indicating X-linked dominant.
X-linked recessive would rarely give all affected daughters from an affected father with unaffected mothers.

items.prompt: Two unaffected parents have an affected child. Which observation would most strongly argue against autosomal recessive inheritance and for X-linked recessive inheritance in the family?

options.label: Affected individuals appear in several generations, with both sexes affected
Only males are affected, and affected males are related through females
The parents of affected children are first cousins, and both sexes are affected
Males and females are affected equally, and unaffected carriers are common

rubric: Male-only affected pattern transmitted through carrier females points to X-linked recessive.
Consanguinity favours autosomal recessive.

items.prompt: A mutation in a gene changes codon `CAG` (Gln) to `UAG` in the mRNA. Compared with a mutation changing it to `CAA`, why is the first likely to be far more damaging?

options.label: UAG is a missense change that swaps Gln for a different amino acid, while CAA is a nonsense change
UAG inserts an extra amino acid into the chain, while CAA removes one amino acid from it
UAG shifts the reading frame for every downstream codon, while CAA leaves the frame intact
UAG is a stop codon that truncates the protein, while CAA still codes for Gln

rubric: Nonsense creates premature termination; CAA is silent.
Frameshift claims confuse substitution with insertion or deletion.

items.prompt: A population is in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium for a locus with alleles A and a. Surveys later find far fewer heterozygotes than expected from allele frequencies, with an excess of both homozygotes. Which cause best explains this?

options.label: Heterozygote advantage
Random mating
Inbreeding or population substructure
Gene flow evenly across the population

rubric: Inbreeding reduces heterozygotes below 2pq while allele frequencies stay the same.
Heterozygote advantage would raise heterozygote frequency.

items.prompt: In a cross between two heterozygous plants (AaBb x AaBb), the observed phenotype ratio is 9:3:4 instead of 9:3:3:1. Which explanations are consistent with this ratio? Select all that apply.

options.label: Incomplete dominance at both loci, giving three phenotype classes at each gene
Recessive epistasis, where homozygous bb masks the expression of A, merging two classes
Recessive epistasis at the other locus, where homozygous aa masks the expression of B, merging two classes
Complete linkage between the two genes, so only parental combinations are produced in the gametes

rubric: 9:3:4 is the classic result of recessive epistasis, with two classes merging.
Linkage and incomplete dominance would give different ratios.

items.prompt: A researcher crosses true-breeding red-flowered plants with true-breeding white-flowered plants. All F1 offspring are pink, and the F2 shows red, pink and white in a 1:2:1 ratio. A colleague claims this disproves Mendel's segregation. What is the best analysis?

options.label: The 1:2:1 ratio means two linked genes are being inherited together, so independent segregation fails
Segregation is violated because the pink F1 blended the parental alleles and they were lost
Segregation still holds; the heterozygote shows an intermediate phenotype, which is incomplete dominance
The result shows the trait is X-linked, so the ratio reflects sex-specific allele transmission in the F2

rubric: The 1:2:1 ratio shows alleles separate intact; only dominance relations differ.
Blending would not recover red and white in the F2.

items.prompt: A testcross of AaBb x aabb gives 42 AaBb, 41 aabb, 9 Aabb and 8 aaBb offspring. What is the recombination frequency, and what does the pattern show about the heterozygous parent?

options.label: 17%; the genes are linked and the parent carried them in coupling (AB/ab)
83%; the genes assort independently because most progeny are parental types
50%; the genes are on separate chromosomes because all four classes appear
17%; the genes are linked and the parent carried them in repulsion (Ab/aB)

rubric: Parental classes (AaBb, aabb) are most common, so the parent was AB/ab; recombinants are 17 of 100.
Distractors confuse coupling with repulsion or treat the presence of all four classes as independent assortment.

items.prompt: In a pedigree (assume full penetrance), two unaffected parents have an affected daughter. Which inference is best supported?

options.label: Autosomal dominant; one parent carried the allele, and it was not expressed in that parent but was in the daughter
X-linked recessive; the mother is a carrier and the father's X chromosome contributed the second copy, unaffected
Y-linked; the allele passed from the father to the daughter and was not expressed in him until she inherited it
Autosomal recessive; both parents are carriers, so X-linked recessive is excluded

rubric: An affected daughter needs two copies; X-linked recessive would require an affected father, and a fully penetrant dominant allele would show in a parent.
Distractors misapply X-linked, dominant or Y-linked logic.

items.prompt: A sample of 100 diploid individuals has genotype counts AA = 50, Aa = 20, aa = 30. Comparing these to Hardy-Weinberg expectations, what is the best interpretation?

options.label: Deficit of homozygotes, because new mutation raises the number of Aa individuals above expectation
Excess homozygotes: expected Aa is 48 but 20 were seen, suggesting inbreeding or population substructure
Equilibrium holds, because allele frequencies p = 0.6 and q = 0.4 sum to 1 and so fix genotype counts
Excess heterozygotes, because only heterozygote advantage can keep 20 Aa individuals in the sample

rubric: p = 0.6, q = 0.4 gives expected 36 AA, 48 Aa, 16 aa; the observed deficit of heterozygotes points to nonrandom mating or substructure.
Distractors treat allele frequencies alone as proof of equilibrium or invoke irrelevant forces.

items.prompt: In a pedigree for a rare dominant condition, a woman is unaffected, but her mother and her son are both affected. Which explanation is the most parsimonious?

options.label: Y-linked inheritance: the allele passed through her mother's line to her son
Recessive inheritance: she is a carrier and her husband was also a carrier
Reduced penetrance: she carries the allele but does not express it
A new mutation in her son that is unrelated to her mother's condition

rubric: An unaffected link between two affected relatives in a dominant trait is best explained by reduced penetrance.
Distractors invoke an impossible Y-linkage, abandon the dominant model, or require coincidence.

items.prompt: A pedigree shows all children of affected mothers affected, and no children of affected fathers affected. What best distinguishes this from X-linked dominant inheritance?

options.label: X-linked dominant would give affected mothers only affected daughters, but here affected mothers also have affected sons, so the pattern is autosomal
X-linked dominant would give affected fathers all affected daughters, but none are
X-linked dominant and this pattern are identical, since both are passed on mainly through mothers to children of both sexes
X-linked dominant would give affected fathers only affected sons, but here no sons of fathers are affected

rubric: Affected fathers pass their X to all daughters, so X-linked dominant predicts affected daughters; their absence indicates mitochondrial inheritance.
Distractors misstate which offspring receive the father's X or claim the patterns are equivalent.

items.prompt: A dihybrid F1 self-cross gives an F2 ratio of 9:3:4. Which conclusions follow? Select all that apply.

options.label: The two genes are tightly linked in coupling
The F1 plants were heterozygous at both loci
Two genes are segregating independently
Homozygous recessive at one gene masks the phenotype of the other gene
A single gene with codominant alleles controls the trait

rubric: 9:3:4 is a modified 9:3:3:1 with recessive epistasis, requiring two independently assorting genes and a double heterozygote F1.
Single-gene codominance gives 1:2:1, and tight linkage would distort the ratio away from 9:3:4.

items.prompt: A fly geneticist crosses a true-breeding red-eyed female with a white-eyed male; all F1 are red-eyed. The reciprocal cross (white-eyed female x red-eyed male) gives red-eyed daughters and white-eyed sons. Which interpretation best fits both crosses?

options.label: White is X-linked dominant; daughters of white mothers should be white but sampling hid this
White is X-linked recessive; sons inherit their only X from the mother and so match her phenotype
White is autosomal recessive; the reciprocal difference comes from maternal cytoplasmic factors
White is Y-linked; sons of white-eyed mothers receive the trait through the egg cytoplasm

rubric: Different outcomes in reciprocal crosses indicate X-linkage; sons take the mother's X, so white sons come from white mothers.
Distractors propose autosomal, dominant or Y-linked explanations that fail to predict the observed sex-specific pattern.

items.prompt: A monohybrid F2 gives 290 dominant and 110 recessive offspring (n = 400). Using chi-square (critical value 3.84 at p = 0.05, df = 1) against a 3:1 expectation, which conclusion is best supported?

options.label: Chi-square is about 1.33, below 3.84, so the data fit 3:1 and chance can explain the deviation
Chi-square is about 1.33, above the critical value for df = 2, so the 3:1 hypothesis is rejected as a poor fit
Chi-square is about 1.33, which is low enough to prove the cross segregates exactly 3:1 for a single gene
Chi-square is about 4.0, above 3.84, so the deviation is significant and the 3:1 ratio is rejected

rubric: Expected 300:100 gives (100/300) + (100/100) = 1.33, which is below 3.84 with df = 1, so 3:1 is not rejected.
Distractors claim proof, use the wrong df, or miscalculate the statistic.

items.prompt: Two healthy carriers of a fully penetrant autosomal recessive allele have two unaffected children and reason that the third child has a risk below 25%. Which critique is best?

options.label: Flawed: each conception is independent, so the risk stays 1/4 whatever the earlier children's phenotypes were
Partly valid: the risk falls to 1/8 because two earlier unaffected children halve the chance again
Valid: two unaffected children show the 3:1 expectation is being used up, so the remaining risk falls
Flawed: the risk is 1/2 because both parents are carriers and each child is either a carrier or affected

rubric: Mendelian segregation is independent at each conception, so the risk remains 1/4.
Distractors reflect the gambler's fallacy or confuse risk of being affected with risk of being a carrier.

items.prompt: Genes A and C lie about 40 cM apart, with marker B between them. The goal is the most accurate map distance for A to C. Which approach is best?

options.label: Sum the A-B and B-C distances from separate crosses, since double crossovers make the direct A-C value too low
Use the direct A-C recombination frequency, since it reflects the true number of crossovers across the interval
Measure A-C recombination directly in a very large progeny, since sample size removes any systematic error
Halve the direct A-C value, since multiple crossovers inflate recombination frequency at long intervals

rubric: Double crossovers restore parental combinations, so recombination frequency underestimates long distances; summing short intervals corrects this.
Distractors assume sample size fixes a systematic bias, or reverse the direction of the bias.

items.prompt: A small isolated population of an endangered species is losing heterozygosity through drift. Criteria: restore variation, avoid swamping local alleles. Which management step is best?

options.label: Introduce a large number of individuals from a distant population at once, since this restores variation immediately and gives the population the most new alleles
Prevent all breeding between close relatives, since this restores variation by stopping inbreeding from reducing allele diversity
Introduce a few unrelated migrants each generation, since this adds new alleles gradually while local ones persist
Cull individuals showing deleterious recessive phenotypes, since this removes harmful alleles and lets the remaining population recover variation

rubric: Modest, repeated gene flow restores variation while retaining local adaptation.
Culling affects rare alleles hidden in heterozygotes poorly; mass introduction risks swamping; avoiding relatives does not add alleles.

items.prompt: Which mutation in a gene's coding sequence is most likely to cause complete loss of function, judged by how much it disrupts the protein product?

options.label: A conservative missense change in a poorly conserved loop, which swaps one similar amino acid for another
An in-frame three-base deletion in a non-conserved linker, which removes one amino acid
A synonymous substitution in the middle exon, which alters a codon but keeps the amino acid
A single-base deletion 20 codons after the start, which shifts the reading frame and creates an early stop

rubric: An early frameshift truncates the protein and often triggers decay of the transcript, giving a null allele.
The other options leave the protein largely intact.

items.prompt: A study samples 20 people from one isolated village and finds an allele at 30% frequency, concluding it is common worldwide. Which are valid criticisms? Select all that apply.

options.label: Hardy-Weinberg theory prohibits any allele from exceeding 25%
Isolated villages can differ from the world through founder effects and drift
Sampling a single non-representative population does not support a worldwide claim
Allele frequencies cannot be estimated from genotype counts at all
The sample is small, so the estimate has a wide margin of error

rubric: Small samples, founder effects and unrepresentative sampling all weaken a global generalisation.
Genotype counts do yield allele frequencies, and Hardy-Weinberg sets no such cap.

items.prompt: A breeder works with a small dog breed where a fatal recessive disease allele has frequency about 0.1, and a DNA test exists. Criteria: cut affected pups while keeping genetic diversity. Which plan is best?

options.label: Stop breeding affected dogs only, since affected dogs carry the allele and removing them eliminates it from the whole population
Outcross once to another breed and then close the registry, since new alleles dilute the disease allele and fix the problem permanently
Remove every carrier from breeding immediately, since this gives the fastest fall in allele frequency across the whole breed
Test all breeding dogs and mate carriers only with non-carriers, gradually replacing carriers with non-carrier offspring

rubric: Carrier-by-non-carrier matings produce no affected pups and keep the carriers' other genes in the pool.
Culling all carriers causes a bottleneck, affected dogs are only a small share of alleles, and one outcross does not remove the allele.

items.prompt: A researcher pools blood samples from two isolated villages into one dataset. At a neutral locus the pooled sample shows fewer heterozygotes than 2pq predicts, although mating within each village is random. Which explanation is best?

options.label: Allele frequencies differ between the villages, so pooling them produces a heterozygote deficit relative to expectations from pooled frequencies
Strong overdominance in both villages is maintaining excess homozygotes at this locus, because selection favours the homozygous genotypes there
Recurrent mutation is converting heterozygotes into homozygotes faster than random mating can restore Hardy-Weinberg proportions in each village
Any heterozygote deficit proves assortative mating inside each village, because random mating always yields exactly 2pq in every sample

rubric: Pooling subpopulations with different allele frequencies lowers heterozygosity below the pooled 2pq (Wahlund effect).
Distractors invoke selection, mutation or assortative mating, which don't fit a neutral locus with random mating within each village.

items.prompt: A student finds 50% recombination between two loci in a testcross and concludes they must lie on different chromosomes. Which critique is best?

options.label: Correct, because linked loci on one chromosome always show recombination clearly below 50% regardless of how far apart they are on the map
Incorrect, because loci on different chromosomes should give recombination above 50% owing to independent assortment of the homologues
Flawed, because distant loci on one chromosome also reach about 50% through multiple crossovers, so the data cannot separate the cases
Incorrect, because exactly 50% recombination shows tight linkage with one obligatory crossover occurring between the two loci every meiosis

rubric: Multiple crossovers saturate recombination frequency at 50% for distant syntenic loci, mimicking independent assortment.
Distractors treat 50% as diagnostic of chromosome identity or of tight linkage.

items.prompt: In a pedigree, every daughter of an affected father is affected and none of his sons are. Affected mothers pass the trait to about half of their sons and half of their daughters, with no skipped generations. Which mode of inheritance fits best?

options.label: X-linked recessive, because daughters of affected fathers are always carriers and the trait skips generations through them
X-linked dominant, because fathers give their only X to all daughters and no sons, and affected mothers transmit it to half
Autosomal dominant with full penetrance, because affected fathers should pass the allele to sons and daughters equally often
Mitochondrial, because the pattern depends on the sex of the transmitting parent and so follows the maternal line only

rubric: Father-to-daughter-only transmission with no skipping indicates X-linked dominance.
Autosomal dominant predicts affected sons; X-linked recessive skips generations; mitochondrial can't pass from father to daughters.

items.prompt: A recessive disease has incidence 1 in 10,000 in a community with substantial consanguinity. A counselor sets q = 0.01 and quotes a carrier frequency of about 2%. How should this estimate be judged?

options.label: Likely an overestimate, because inbreeding raises affected frequency above q^2, so the true q and carrier rate are lower than quoted
Sound, because the square root of incidence gives q under any mating pattern, and carriers then follow directly from 2pq
Unreliable in either direction, because consanguinity changes allele frequencies themselves, so incidence says nothing about carriers
Likely an underestimate, because inbreeding reduces the number of affected people and so hides alleles carried by heterozygotes

rubric: With inbreeding coefficient F, incidence is q^2 + Fpq, so taking the square root of incidence overestimates q.
Distractors ignore inbreeding or reverse its effect on homozygote frequency.

items.prompt: Researchers collect only families identified through an affected child, all from carrier x carrier matings, and find 40% of siblings affected. They conclude the trait is not simple autosomal recessive. How should this be evaluated?

options.label: Flawed, because families found through an affected child miss carrier couples with no affected children, inflating the ratio above 25%
Flawed, because every carrier couple must produce exactly one affected child in four, so a 40% figure shows a counting error
Flawed, because carrier x carrier matings should yield 50% affected children, so 40% suggests reduced penetrance of the recessive allele
Sound, because 40% differs from 25% by far more than chance in a large sample of families, so the recessive model must be rejected

rubric: Ascertainment through affected children biases the sibling ratio upward; correction is needed.
Distractors misread Mendelian ratios as per-family certainties or as 50%.

items.prompt: A variant is proposed as the cause of a rare, highly penetrant dominant disorder (prevalence 1 in 50,000). Which findings weaken this claim? Select all that apply.

options.label: The variant occurs in about 2% of well-phenotyped adults who are past the usual age of onset
The variant arose de novo in an affected proband and is absent from both unaffected parents
The variant changes an amino acid residue conserved across vertebrate species
A cell-based functional assay shows protein activity indistinguishable from wild type

rubric: A carrier frequency far above disease prevalence in unaffected adults, and normal function, both argue against causality.
De novo origin and conservation are supporting evidence, not counter-evidence.

items.prompt: A mouse colony crosses two yellow-coated mice repeatedly and always gets yellow and non-yellow pups in a 2:1 ratio. Litters are about 25% smaller than in non-yellow x non-yellow crosses. Yellow x non-yellow crosses give 1:1 litters of normal size. Which interpretation best fits the data?

options.label: Yellow is codominant with non-yellow, so heterozygotes and homozygotes are scored together and produce a distorted 2:1 phenotype ratio
Yellow is dominant for coat colour but homozygous lethal in utero, so all surviving yellow mice are heterozygous
Meiotic drive favours non-yellow gametes in yellow parents, which would also explain the reduced litter sizes seen in these crosses
Yellow shows incomplete penetrance in one third of heterozygotes, so they appear non-yellow, with no effect on litter size

rubric: A 2:1 ratio with 25% fewer pups indicates the homozygous dominant class dies before birth.
Distractors can't explain both the ratio and smaller litters, or the normal 1:1 backcross.

items.prompt: Two true-breeding fly lines show the same recessive eye phenotype. You need a design that decides, from one cross scored in the F1 generation, whether the mutations are in the same gene. Which design meets this?

options.label: Cross each line to wild type and score the F1; wild-type F1 in both crosses shows the mutations affect the same gene
Cross each line to wild type, then testcross the F1; a 1:1 ratio in both testcrosses shows the mutations affect the same gene
Cross the two homozygous lines to each other; mutant F1 means the same gene, wild-type F1 means different genes
Self each line and compare F2 ratios; a 3:1 wild-type to mutant ratio in both lines shows the mutations affect the same gene

rubric: A complementation test of homozygous mutants gives a single-generation answer.
Distractors use crosses to wild type, which can't compare the two mutations and need extra generations.

items.prompt: A zoo holds a captive population founded by 20 unrelated individuals. The goal is to retain about 90% of founder gene diversity for 100 years at a fixed small size with equal sexes. Which breeding plan meets this?

options.label: Breed the individuals in best condition most often, since selection for fitness preserves the alleles that matter most in captivity
Pair by lowest mean kinship, equalise the contribution of each founder lineage, and hold population size constant to limit drift
Pair the closest relatives so deleterious alleles are purged early, then hold the surviving lines at constant size across the century
Keep each founder's descendants in separate groups with no exchange, so every lineage is protected from loss by drift

rubric: Minimising mean kinship and equalising founder representation slows loss of gene diversity.
Distractors favour selection, purging by inbreeding, or isolation, all of which erode diversity.

items.prompt: A woman's mother is a known carrier of an X-linked recessive disease, and her brother is affected. She has two unaffected sons. Which plan gives her correct updated carrier probability?

options.label: Weight carrier prior 1/2 by 1/4 for two unaffected sons, non-carrier prior 1/2 by 1, then normalise to get 1/5
Keep the prior of 1/2, because the status of her sons is independent of whether she carries the allele
Multiply the prior 1/2 by 1/4 for two unaffected sons and report 1/8 without comparing it to the alternative
Average the prior 1/2 with the 1/4 chance of two unaffected sons and report a posterior of about 3/8

rubric: Bayesian updating: carrier 1/8 versus non-carrier 1/2 gives 1/5.
Distractors ignore the evidence, skip normalisation or average probabilities.

items.prompt: A lab must maintain a recessive lethal allele `l` on a fly chromosome as a permanent stock without scoring or selecting each generation. Which design meets this?

options.label: Keep `l` as a homozygous stock and rely on the few survivors to carry the allele into each new generation of the culture
Cross `l/+` flies among themselves each generation and discard all wild-type progeny by hand to keep the allele in the culture
Cross `l/+` flies to a stock carrying a visible dominant marker on the homolog, then pick marked heterozygotes each generation to propagate the line
Keep `l` heterozygous with a balancer chromosome: inversions block recombination, a dominant marker tags it, and it is homozygous lethal

rubric: A balancer suppresses recombination and its homozygous lethality means only l/Balancer flies persist, so the stock self-maintains.
Distractors need constant manual selection or don't work.

items.prompt: A case-control GWAS draws cases mostly from one ancestry and controls mostly from another. It reports hundreds of hits at ancestry-differentiated loci. Which revision removes the confounding without discarding samples?

options.label: Restrict the analysis to common variants with minor allele frequency above 5%, where allele frequency differences between ancestries are assumed to be small enough
Apply a stricter Bonferroni threshold across all tested variants so that only the strongest associations survive, which filters out weaker ancestry-driven signals
Double the sample size using the same sampling scheme, so that the spurious ancestry-driven associations average out as statistical power increases
Add top principal components of genome-wide genotypes, or a relatedness matrix, to adjust for ancestry

rubric: Adjusting for ancestry through principal components or mixed models addresses population stratification directly.
Distractors alter thresholds or sample size, which leave the ancestry-disease correlation in place.

items.prompt: You must determine the order of three linked genes from one experiment. Which elements belong in a design that meets this goal? Select all that apply.

options.label: Testcross a triple heterozygote to a triple homozygous recessive
Cross two homozygous dominant parents and read the order from F1 ratios
Score progeny at only two loci at a time to simplify the counting
Score all eight phenotypic classes in a large progeny so double-crossover classes appear
Compare parental and double-crossover classes; the gene whose allele switches is in the middle

rubric: A three-point testcross with full scoring and a large sample reveals the rare double crossovers; the switched gene is the middle one.
Scoring two loci at a time or crossing homozygous parents loses the information needed.

items.prompt: A team identifies a candidate gene for a neural defect and plans to knock it out with CRISPR in mouse embryos, then compare the founder phenotype with the human syndrome. A reviewer says this design cannot establish causality. What is the most important element missing?

options.label: A comparison of mouse and human brain size, to confirm that the species have comparable neural development
A larger number of founders from the same guide RNA, to establish that the phenotype is seen in most injected animals
A second independent allele, or a rescue transgene, to show the phenotype follows the gene and not off-target edits
Sequencing of the human patients' parents, to confirm that the human variant is inherited and not de novo in the proband

rubric: Independent alleles or rescue separate the gene's effect from off-target mutations.
Distractors improve numbers or human data but don't link the mouse phenotype to the gene.
